\section[comenzar]{comenzar — to begin, to start}

\label{lesson:ES-C542-comenzar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to go on, then the Spanish for to go by.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: comenzar}
\textbf{comenzar} — \textquotedblleft{}to begin, to start\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La película comenzó a las nueve.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The film began at nine.}
\end{quote}

Stem change: \emph{comienza}, \emph{comienzan}. A little more formal than \emph{empezar}. \emph{Comenzar a} + infinitive.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{comenzar} is inherited from spoken Latin \emph{*cominitiāre} (EtymDB), built on \emph{com-} and \emph{initiāre} 'to begin', from \emph{initium} 'a beginning'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{comenzar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{comenzar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{comenzar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to go on, then the Spanish for to go by, then say \emph{comenzar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does comenzar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To begin, to start\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[iniciar]{iniciar — to launch, to start, to begin}

\label{lesson:ES-C542-iniciar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to go by, then the Spanish for to begin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: iniciar}
\textbf{iniciar} — \textquotedblleft{}to launch, to start, to begin\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La policía inició una investigación.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The police started an investigation.}
\end{quote}

Formal; common in the news. \emph{Iniciar sesión} — to log in.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{iniciar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{initiāre} 'to begin, to initiate' (EtymDB), built on \emph{initium} 'a going in, a beginning'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{iniciar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{iniciar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{iniciar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to go by, then the Spanish for to begin, then say \emph{iniciar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does iniciar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To launch, to start, to begin\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[el comienzo]{el comienzo — the beginning, the start}

\label{lesson:ES-C542-comienzo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to begin, then the Spanish for to launch.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el comienzo}
\textbf{el comienzo} — \textquotedblleft{}the beginning, the start\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El comienzo del libro es muy lento.

\emph{comienzo} is built on \emph{comenzar} (EtymDB), which comes from spoken Latin \emph{*cominitiāre}, from \emph{initium} 'a beginning'.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[el arranque]{el arranque — the start; the outburst}

\label{lesson:ES-C542-arranque}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to launch, then the Spanish for the beginning.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el arranque}
\textbf{el arranque} — \textquotedblleft{}the start; the outburst\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El arranque del curso fue difícil.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The start of the school year was hard.}
\end{quote}

A car's starter is also \emph{el arranque}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{arranque} is built on \emph{arrancar} 'to pull out, to start'. The origin of \emph{arrancar} is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[finalizar]{finalizar — to end, to finish}

\label{lesson:ES-C542-finalizar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the beginning, then the Spanish for the start.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: finalizar}
\textbf{finalizar} — \textquotedblleft{}to end, to finish\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La reunión finalizó a las seis.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The meeting ended at six.}
\end{quote}

Formal; in speech people say \emph{terminar} or \emph{acabar}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{finalizar} is built on \emph{final} with the ending \emph{-izar}. \emph{Final} comes from Latin \emph{fīnālis}, from \emph{fīnis} 'end' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the beginning, then the Spanish for the start, then say \emph{finalizar} again
